Otherwise add both-side attributes one at a time, then in pairs, testing closure and skipping supersets of keys already found.
Check the final list is an antichain: no key contains another.
problemTypes.trap: Stopping at the first key found; relations with cyclic FDs such as A → B, B → A usually have several keys.

problemTypes.title: Highest normal form of a relation
recipe: Find every candidate key and list the prime attributes.
Split each FD to single-attribute right sides and drop trivial ones.
For each FD X → A: X superkey passes BCNF; else A prime passes 3NF only; else X inside a key fails 2NF; else it fails 3NF.
Before reporting 2NF, compute (K − {b})⁺ for every key K and every b ∈ K; any non-prime attribute in that closure is a partial dependency that the given FDs may hide.
Report the weakest verdict across all checks.
problemTypes.trap: Calling a relation 2NF-violating because an FD has a partial-key left side when its right side is prime; prime right sides never break 2NF or 3NF.

problemTypes.title: Lossless join and dependency preservation of a given decomposition
recipe: Lossless, two pieces: compute (R₁ ∩ R₂)⁺ and see whether it contains R₁ or R₂.
Lossless, more pieces: merge two pieces that pass the test, repeat, or run the chase tableau.
Preservation: an FD inside one piece is kept; for one that spans pieces run the projected-closure loop and check the right side appears.
problemTypes.trap: Assuming a lossless decomposition is dependency-preserving, or calling an FD lost just because no single piece contains all its attributes.

problemTypes.title: Canonical cover or equivalence of FD sets
recipe: Split right sides into single attributes and remove duplicates.
For each multi-attribute left side, drop an attribute B when the right side is in (X − B)⁺.
Drop each FD whose right side is still derivable from the others.
For equivalence, test every FD of one set by closure under the other, both ways.
problemTypes.trap: Removing redundant FDs before shrinking left sides, which can leave a redundant FD behind.

problemTypes.title: Count superkeys from the candidate keys
recipe: Find every candidate key first.
Each key K contributes 2^(n − |K|) supersets.
Subtract the overlaps by inclusion–exclusion on the unions of keys.
problemTypes.trap: Adding the per-key counts without subtracting superkeys that contain two keys at once.

problemTypes.title: 3NF synthesis or BCNF decomposition result
recipe: 3NF: take a canonical cover, make one relation per left side, add a candidate-key relation if none contains a key.
BCNF: pick a violating X → Y, split into X ∪ Y and R − (Y − X), and recurse on each piece.
State which properties hold: 3NF synthesis is lossless and preserving; BCNF splitting is lossless only.
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting the key relation in 3NF synthesis, which leaves the decomposition lossy.

problemTypes.title: Which FDs does a given instance satisfy
recipe: For each candidate FD X → Y, group rows by their X values.
The FD fails if any group shows two different Y values; otherwise it holds on this instance.
problemTypes.trap: Treating an FD as satisfied because most rows agree; a single conflicting pair breaks it.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D, E, F, G) has the FDs AB → CD, AF → D, DE → F, C → G, F → E, G → A. How many attributes does the closure (CF)⁺ contain?
questions.explanation: Start with {C, F}. C → G adds G; G → A adds A; F → E adds E; AF → D now fires and adds D. DE → F adds nothing new, and AB → CD never fires because B is never added. (CF)⁺ = {A, C, D, E, F, G}: 6 attributes, so CF is not a superkey.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D, E, H) has the FDs A → BC, E → HA, BC → D, D → E. What are all the candidate keys of R?
questions.explanation: H appears only on a right side, so it is in no key. A⁺: A → BC, BC → D, D → E, E → HA gives all six. E⁺ = {E, H, A} then B, C, D: all. D⁺ = {D, E} then H, A, B, C: all. (BC)⁺ = {B, C, D, E, H, A}: all, and B⁺ = {B}, C⁺ = {C}, so BC is minimal. Any other key must avoid A, D, E and the pair BC, leaving only subsets of {B, H} or {C, H}; (BH)⁺ = {B, H} and (CH)⁺ = {C, H}. So the keys are exactly {A}, {D}, {E}, {B, C}.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D, E) has the FDs AB → CD, D → E, E → A. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.explanation: B is on no right side, so it is in every key; C is only on a right side, so it is in no key. B⁺ = {B}. Adding one both-side attribute: (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D} then E; (BD)⁺ = {B, D, E, A} then C; (BE)⁺ = {B, E, A} then C, D. All three equal R and none contains another. Any larger candidate would contain one of them. So there are 3 keys: AB, BD, BE.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D) has the FDs AB → CD and D → A. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: B is on no right side. (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D} and (BD)⁺ = {B, D, A, C}, while B⁺ = {B}, so the keys are AB and BD; prime attributes are A, B, D. AB → CD has a key on the left. D → A has a non-superkey left side (D⁺ = {D, A}), so BCNF fails, but A is prime, so 3NF holds. Highest normal form: 3NF.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D) has the FDs AB → C and B → D. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.explanation: A and B appear on no right side, and (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, so AB is the only key and C, D are non-prime. B → D makes the non-prime D depend on B, a proper subset of the key: a partial dependency. R is in 1NF but not 2NF.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C) has the FDs AB → C and C → B. It is decomposed on C → B into R₁(C, B) and R₂(A, C). Which statement is true?
options: The decomposition is lossless and dependency-preserving
The decomposition is lossless but not dependency-preserving
The decomposition is dependency-preserving but lossy
The decomposition is neither lossless nor dependency-preserving
questions.explanation: R₁ ∩ R₂ = {C} and C⁺ = {C, B} = R₁, so the join is lossless. Projected FDs: C → B on R₁ and nothing non-trivial on R₂ (A⁺ = {A}, C⁺ ∩ {A, C} = {C}). From C → B alone, (AB)⁺ = {A, B}, so AB → C is lost and needs a join to enforce. This is the standard case where BCNF costs dependency preservation.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D, E) has the FDs AB → C, C → D, B → E. Which decomposition of R is lossless?
questions.explanation: Option 1: (A, B, C) ∩ (C, D) = {C} and C → D makes C a key of (C, D), so they join losslessly into (A, B, C, D); that ∩ (B, E) = {B} and B → E makes B a key of (B, E): lossless. Option 2 has an empty intersection. Option 3 shares C, but C⁺ = {C, D} contains neither {A, C, D} nor {B, C, E}. Option 4 shares B, but B⁺ = {B, E} contains neither piece.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D) has the FDs A → B, B → C, C → D. It is decomposed into R₁(A, B), R₂(A, C) and R₃(A, D). Which statements are true?
options: The decomposition preserves every FD of F
Each of R₁, R₂ and R₃ is in BCNF
B → C can be enforced inside a single relation of the decomposition
questions.explanation: A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, so A is a key of every piece. R₁ ∩ R₂ = {A} determines R₁, so R₁ ⋈ R₂ is lossless; its intersection with R₃ is again {A}: lossless. The projected FDs are A → B, A → C and A → D only, since B⁺ ∩ {A, B} = {B} and so on. Under these, B⁺ = {B}, so B → C and C → D are lost, and no piece contains both B and C. Every two-attribute relation is in BCNF.

questions.stem: F = {A → BC, B → C, AB → D, AC → D, D → B} over R(A, B, C, D). How many FDs does a canonical cover of F contain?
questions.explanation: Split: A → B, A → C, B → C, AB → D, AC → D, D → B. Left sides: A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, so AB → D and AC → D both shrink to A → D (B⁺ = {B, C} and C⁺ = {C} do not reach D). Now {A → B, A → C, B → C, A → D, D → B}. Drop A → B: A → D → B still gives B. Drop A → C: A → D → B → C still gives C. A → D, D → B and B → C are each needed (A⁺, D⁺, B⁺ shrink without them). The cover {A → D, D → B, B → C} has 3 FDs, and every order of removals reaches this same cover.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D, E, F) has the FDs A → BCDEF and BC → A. How many superkeys does R have?
questions.explanation: D, E and F appear only on right sides. A⁺ = R, and (BC)⁺ = {B, C, A, D, E, F} = R while B⁺ = {B}, C⁺ = {C}; any key without A needs both B and C, so the keys are {A} and {B, C}. Supersets of A: 2⁵ = 32. Supersets of BC: 2⁴ = 16. Supersets of both, i.e. of ABC: 2³ = 8. Superkeys = 32 + 16 − 8 = 40.

questions.stem: An instance of r(A, B, C) has exactly four tuples: (1, p, x), (1, p, y), (2, q, x), (3, q, x). Which FDs does this instance satisfy?
questions.explanation: A → B: the only repeated A value is 1, and both rows have B = p, so it holds. C → B: C = x appears with B = p and B = q, so it fails. AC → B: the AC pairs (1, x), (1, y), (2, x), (3, x) are all distinct, so it holds trivially on this instance. B → C: B = p appears with C = x and C = y, so it fails.

questions.stem: Only X → Y is given, for arbitrary attribute sets X, Y and Z. Which FD can NOT be inferred from it?
questions.explanation: XZ → YZ is augmentation by Z, and decomposing it gives XZ → Y. Augmenting X → Y by X gives X → XY. X → YZ would need X → Z, which is not given: two tuples equal on X and Y but different on Z satisfy X → Y and violate X → YZ.

questions.stem: R(Course, Instructor, Textbook) records, for each course, every combination of its instructors and its textbooks; the instructors and textbooks of a course are independent of each other, and no FD other than trivial ones holds. Which statement is true?
options: R violates BCNF because Course → Instructor holds
R is in BCNF but not in 4NF
R is in 4NF because every attribute is prime
questions.explanation: With only trivial FDs, the single key is all three attributes and R is in BCNF (hence 3NF). Course →→ Instructor is a non-trivial MVD (Instructor ⊄ Course and Course ∪ Instructor ≠ R) whose left side is not a superkey, so 4NF fails. Course → Instructor does not hold, since a course has several instructors. Decompose into (Course, Instructor) and (Course, Textbook).

questions.stem: R(A, B, C) has F = {A → B, B → C, A → C}. Count the FDs X → Y in F⁺ where X and Y are both non-empty subsets of {A, B, C}, trivial FDs included.
questions.explanation: For a fixed non-empty X, X → Y is in F⁺ exactly when Y is a non-empty subset of X⁺, giving 2^|X⁺| − 1 choices. A⁺ = {A, B, C}: 7. B⁺ = {B, C}: 3. C⁺ = {C}: 1. AB⁺, AC⁺ and ABC⁺ are all of R: 7 each. BC⁺ = {B, C}: 3. Total 7 + 3 + 1 + 7 + 7 + 3 + 7 = 35.

questions.stem: R(A, B, C, D, E, F) has the canonical cover {A → B, BC → D, AC → E, F → A}. Which schema does the 3NF synthesis algorithm produce?
questions.explanation: One relation per left side: (A, B), (B, C, D), (A, C, E), (F, A). C and F are on no right side, so every key contains both; (CF)⁺ = {C, F} → A → B, then BC → D and AC → E give all of R, so CF is the only key. No relation contains both C and F, so (C, F) is added. Without it the schema is lossy; merging A → B with AC → E is wrong because the left sides differ.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: Every relation with exactly two attributes is in BCNF
The BCNF decomposition algorithm always produces a lossless decomposition
A relation in which every attribute is prime is always in BCNF
Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
questions.explanation: With two attributes A, B the only possible non-trivial FDs are A → B and B → A, and either one makes its left side a key, so BCNF holds. Each BCNF split shares X and X is a key of X ∪ Y, so every step is lossless. R(City, Pincode, Street) with Pincode → City and City Street → Pincode has every attribute prime, yet Pincode → City breaks BCNF. BCNF's condition is the 3NF condition without the prime exception, so it implies 3NF.

pitfalls.text: Augmentation adds the same attributes to both sides. Widening only the left side is also valid, but widening only the right side is not: X → Y never gives X → YZ.
A superkey is not a candidate key until minimality is checked: remove each attribute in turn and confirm the closure drops below R.
3NF tolerates X → A with a non-superkey X when A is prime; that gap is exactly what separates 3NF from BCNF.
Lossless join needs the common attributes to be a superkey of one piece. Some FD among the shared attributes is not enough.
Lossless join and dependency preservation are independent; check both separately for every decomposition.
In 3NF synthesis, add a candidate-key relation only when no synthesized relation already contains a key, and merge FDs that share a left side.
An MVD is not an FD: Course →→ Instructor allows many instructors per course, while Course → Instructor would allow one.
A table instance can disprove an FD but never establish one for the schema; answer instance questions only about the rows shown.

errata.claim: Augmentation adds attributes to both sides, never to only one: X → Y does not imply X → YZ or XZ → Y in general.
errata.correction: XZ → Y always follows from X → Y: augmentation gives XZ → YZ and decomposition then gives XZ → Y (or XZ → X by reflexivity, then transitivity). Only X → YZ is invalid in general.

errata.claim: X is a key if X⁺ = all attributes; X is a superkey if X⁺ ⊇ all attributes.
errata.correction: X⁺ = R is the superkey test. A candidate key additionally needs minimality: no proper subset of X has closure R.

errata.claim: 4NF: BCNF + no multi-valued dependency (MVD) except trivial.
errata.correction: 4NF allows non-trivial MVDs as long as their left side is a superkey: for every non-trivial MVD X →→ Y, X must be a superkey.

errata.claim: Dependency preservation means every original FD can be enforced by checking only one of the decomposed relations.
errata.correction: An FD is preserved when it follows from the union of the FDs projected onto the pieces; it need not fit inside one relation. R(A, B, C) with A → B, B → C, A → C split into (A, B), (B, C) preserves A → C through A → B and B → C.

errata.claim: BCNF decomposition on a violating X → Y replaces Rᵢ by X ∪ Y and Rᵢ − Y.
errata.correction: The second piece is Rᵢ − (Y − X). If Y overlaps X, subtracting all of Y also removes part of X, and the two pieces no longer share X, so losslessness is no longer guaranteed.

errata.claim: F⁺ for F = {A → B, B → C, A → C} is practically infinite with augmentation; counting it is tedious and no number is given.
errata.correction: F⁺ over a finite schema is finite. Over R(A, B, C), with X and Y non-empty and trivial FDs counted, |F⁺| = Σ (2^|X⁺| − 1) = 7 + 3 + 1 + 7 + 7 + 3 + 7 = 35 (43 if empty sides are allowed).

errata.claim: For F_c = {A → B, BC → D, AC → E, F → A}, the key search starts from F as the only left-only attribute.
errata.correction: C is also on no right side, so the mandatory set is {C, F}; its closure is R, which makes CF the unique candidate key with no search needed.

errata.claim: F = {AB → C, A → B} has multiple possible distinct minimal covers, one being {A → B, A → C}.
errata.correction: The minimal cover is unique here: B is extraneous in AB → C because A⁺ = {A, B, C}, while A is not (B⁺ = {B}), and neither A → B nor A → C is redundant. Every order of reduction gives {A → B, A → C}.
